full_judgment:
7. After the close of the examination of the prosecution witnesses, the accused person was examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to which he repeated his innocence and the defence did not adduce any evidence on his behalf. 

 9. On consideration of the evidence on record as well as the facts and circumstances of the case, the learned Special Tribunal Judge, Lakshmipur, found the accused Mohin Uddin guilty under section 19A and 19(f) of the Arms Act and convicted him separately under two sections as stated hereinbefore. 

 11. Mr Mohammad Ismail along with Mr Shihabuddin Mahrnud, the learned Advocates on behalf of the appellant, submits that he has been falsely implicated in this case at the instigation of his enemy; that no pipe gun and cartridges were recovered from him; that the learned Tribunal Judge erred in law in relying solely upon the evidence of the police witnesses in the absence of corroboration by the members of the public; that the police witnesses were partisan witnesses and they were logically interested in securing conviction and sentence of the appellant once he was arrested by them. He further submits that the learned Tribunal Judge missed and overlooked the improbabilities, inconsistencies and contradictions occurring in the testimonies of the police witnesses disproving the prosecution case; that the place and manner of arrest of the appellant as proved by the prosecution suffers from serious contradictions making the prosecution case worthless and incredible; that there is no evidence on record proving that the firearms, ammunition alleged to have been seized from the possession of the appellant were at all used in the gun battle and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is extremely bad in law, inasmuch as that it is unwarranted by the facts and circumstances and against the weight of evidence on record. 

 12. Mrs Umme Kulsum Begum, the learned Deputy Attorney-General along with Mr SM Shahjahan Kabir, learned Assistant Attorney-General for State, on the other hand, submits that the prosecution proved its case against the accused appellant by most consistent, corroborative and overwhelming evidence of competent witnesses. She further submits that the learned Special Tribunal Judge was perfectly justified in convicting and sentencing the accused appellant on the basis of the most cogent and reliable evidence and that his judgment does not suffer from any misreading and non-reading of evidence. She further submits that all the prosecution witnesses are natural, probable and competent witnesses and there is no internal points of falsehood in their evidence on any point and, as such, the impugned judgment calls for no interference by the Court. 

 14. In the face of argument advanced by the learned Advocates of the contending parties, we are now called upon to scrutinise the material evidence in order to come to a proper decision in this appeal. 

 30. PW 9, SI Abdul Matin, deposed corroborating the evidence of PW 1, PW 4 and PW 7, that on 13-7-2001 they went on patrol duty under the leadership of Officer in Charge, Lakshmipur, Sheikh Abdul Mannan and arrested the accused after exchange of fire, with arms and ammunition and other looted goods which were seized through a seizure list in their presence and local witnesses also identified the seizure list. 

 39. These are all the evidence adduced by the prosecution. 

 51. There is no reason why the evidence of police personnel should be discarded simply because they belonged to the police force. They came before the Court and testified to the occurrence. They were fully cross examined. Their evidence is also evidence within the meaning of section 3 of the Evidence Act. 

 52. Now let us see the law regarding procedure of seizing of articles which is envisaged in section 103 of the Code of Criminal Procedure: 

 "103: Search to be made in presence of witnesses (1) Before making a search under this chapter, the officer or other person about to make it shall call upon two or more respectable inhabitants of the locality in which the place to be searched is situated to attend and witness the search and may issue an order in writing to them or any of them so to do. 

 53. In the 'instant case the compliance of the provision of section 103 regarding seizure was followed. The pipe gun and 4 live cartridges were recovered from the waist of the accused in presence of 3 local witnesses beside police personnel. PW 2 Md Siddique Ullah, PW 3 Kamal Uddin and PW 5 Abdul Mannan are local seizure list witnesses who substantially deposed that Sheikh Abdul Mannan, Officer in Charge, Lakshmipur, prepared seizure list in their presence recovering the pipegun and 4 live cartridges from the accused Mohiuddin. PW 1 Sheikh Abdul Mannan proves the seizure list which is marked as Exhibit 1. Though the local witnesses were not present immediately after recovery, it matters little as because there was gun fight between the patrol party and dacoitparty. Officer in Charge Lakshmipur was able to catch one of the dacoits namely, the accused Mohiuddin. It is not possible and natural to remain present of the local witness at that time. 

 54. On reading of evidence of police witnesses; it appears to us that they after seizing the pipe gun and 4 live cartridges and other goods and arrested accused person, they were brought to the locality and prepared the seizure list in presence of the local witnesses. 

 55. There is no legal bar to convict and sentence the accused under Arms Act" mainly on the evidence of Police personnel if there appears no falsehood in their evidence. 

 56. We do not find any bar to convict the accused Mohiuddin on the basis of unimpeachable evidence of the Police witnesses who made the search and seizure. The above view finds support in the case of Nurul Islam vs State report in 1988 BLD 106. 

 57. The object of the provisions of section 103, CrPC is to ensure conducting of search in an impartial way and fair manner and also ensure that there is no planting of incriminating articles by the police or by any other person. There are quite a number of cases where the local witnesses of search and seizure do not support the police out of fear of the accused or of their men or on being gained over or for various other reasons and depose falsely in favour of accused to save the offender from legal punishment. Depending on the facts and circum- stances of each case, a judge certainly may disbelieve a witness of search and seizure if it appears to him that he is deliberately making obliging statements in favour of the accused falsely in order to save him from legal punishment. In view of the provision of section 134 of the Evidence Act which provides that no particular number of witnesses shall in any case be required for the proof of any fact, a Judge may convict an accused solely on the basis of the unimpeachable and unshaken evidence of the officer or person who made the search and seizure disbelieving the evidence, if any, of any witness of search and seizure holding it to be unworthy of credit. But in the present case for the reasons stated above it appears that the witnesses of search and seizure namely PW 2 Siddique Ullah, PW 3 Kamaluddin and PW 5 Abdul Mannan categorically deposed that the arms and ammunition were recovered through seizure list prepared in their presence in which they were also witnesses. Even if the seizure list witnesses do not support the prosecution case, the conviction and sentence under section 19A and 19(f) of the Arms Act can be given solely on the testimonies of the Police personnel. 

 58. We also find support in this regard from the decision in the case of SM Kamal vs State reported in 6 BLC 113, wherein it is held that though the public seizure list witness does not support the prosecution case; there is no bar to convict an appellant on the unimpeachable evidence of Police witnesses. In the instant case, the ingredient of section 19 A and 19(f) have been proved. 

 60. The learned Advocate for the appellant submits that there are some discrepancies in, the evidence of the prosecution. Minor discrepancies are not material since they occur due to individual differences. Where minor discrepancies, not going to the root of the matter, are found in the evidence of natural and probable witnesses, the discrepancies should not be over emphasised. Where the presence of eye-witnesses could not be secured at all, that would not prevent the prosecution from relying on the evidence, though circumstantial in nature, and if such evidence is sufficient to bring home the guilt, the conviction should follow. 

 61. In the case under review the circumstantial evidence are also closely connected which led us to arrive at the irresistible conclusion of the guilt of the accused. 

 62. In the facts and circumstances of the instant case and evidence on record and law endorsed under section 19A and 19(f) of the Arms Act, we are of the considered view that the prosecution has been able to prove the case and has been able to connect the appellant in the commission of offence punishable under section 19 A and 19( f) of the Arms Act beyond any shadow of doubt.
